claims.evidence: This is a control experiment supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claims.claim: Interruption of the connection between capillaries and upstream arterioles prevented elevated K+-induced dilation of upstream arterioles.
claims.source: Additional control studies comparing the dilatory response of upstream arterioles to elevated [K+] application before and after severing capillaries from the upstream arteriole segment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) showed that interruption of this connection prevented elevated [K+]-induced dilation of upstream arterioles (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
claims.evidence: This is a control experiment supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Application of 4-HNE onto capillary extremities dilated upstream arterioles in ex vivo preparations from wild-type mice in a concentration-dependent manner.
claims.source: Application of 4-HNE onto capillary extremities dilated upstream arterioles in ex vivo preparations from wild-type mice (Figure 2B) in a concentration-dependent manner.
claims.evidence: This is supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 2B and C.

claims.claim: The EC50 for 4-HNE-induced dilation of upstream arterioles was 190 nM, and the maximal response was achieved at 1 µM.
claims.source: The EC50 for 4-HNE-induced dilation was 190 nM, and the maximal response was achieved at 1 µM; thus, this latter concentration was used in subsequent investigations (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by concentration-response data shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: Dilation of parenchymal arterioles in response to capillary-applied 4-HNE was significantly attenuated by HC-030031.
claims.source: Dilation of parenchymal arterioles in response to capillary-applied 4-HNE was significantly attenuated by superfusing the ex vivo preparation with HC-030031 (Figure 2B and D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 2B and D.

claims.claim: Application of AITC to capillary beds produced a concentration-dependent dilation of upstream arterioles.
claims.source: Application of the TRPA1-activating compound, allyl isothiocyanate (AITC), to capillary beds also produced a concentration-dependent dilation of upstream arterioles (Video 2).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 2E and Video 2.

claims.claim: The EC50 of AITC-induced arteriole dilation was 6 µM, and the maximal response was achieved at a concentration of 30 µM.
claims.source: The EC50 of AITC-induced arteriole dilation was 6 µM, and the maximal response was achieved at a concentration of 30 µM (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by concentration-response data shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: HC-030031 inhibited upstream dilation in response to AITC (30 µM).
claims.source: HC-030031 also inhibited upstream dilation in response to AITC (30 µM) (Figure 2F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 2F.

claims.claim: The dilatory response of upstream arterioles to stimulation of capillary extremities with AITC was absent after severing the connection between capillaries and the upstream arteriole.
claims.source: In addition, the dilatory response of upstream arterioles to stimulation of capillary extremities with AITC was absent after severing the connection between capillaries and the upstream arteriole (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), providing evidence that this response requires intercellular signal propagation.
claims.evidence: This is supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: In ex vivo preparations obtained from Trpa1-ecKO mice, stimulation of capillaries with elevated K+ evoked dilation of upstream arterioles.
claims.source: In ex vivo preparations obtained from Trpa1-ecKO mice, stimulation of capillaries with elevated [K+] evoked dilation of upstream arterioles (Figure 2G to I)
claims.evidence: This is supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 2G to I.

claims.claim: Neither 4-HNE nor AITC had any effect on upstream arteriole dilation in preparations from Trpa1-ecKO mice at concentrations that produced maximal dilation in control animals.
claims.source: however, neither 4-HNE (Figure 2G and H) nor AITC (Figure 2I) had any effect at concentrations that produced maximal dilation of microvascular preparations from control animals.
claims.evidence: This is supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 2G to I.

claims.claim: Activation of TRPA1 channels in brain capillary endothelial cells produces a signal that propagates to upstream parenchymal arterioles to cause dilation.
claims.source: Together, these data demonstrate that activation of TRPA1 channels in brain capillary endothelial cells produces a signal that propagates to upstream parenchymal arterioles to cause dilation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data from pressure myography experiments.

claims.claim: Endothelial cells of the parenchymal arteriole are encased by a continuous circumferential layer of vascular smooth muscle cells.
claims.source: In agreement with prior studies (Grant et al., 2019; Hartmann et al., 2015; Hill et al., 2015), distinct variations in mural cell morphology were observed in different vascular segments. Endothelial cells of the parenchymal arteriole are encased by a continuous circumferential layer of vascular smooth muscle cells
claims.evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 3A to C and is consistent with prior studies.

claims.claim: Post-arteriole transitional segments are covered by 'ensheathing pericytes' that are morphologically distinct from vascular smooth muscle cells and identified by the classic bump-on-a-log characteristic.
claims.source: whereas post-arteriole transitional segments (i.e. segments between parenchymal arterioles and the dense capillary region) are covered by 'ensheathing pericytes' that are morphologically distinct from vascular smooth muscle cells and identified by the classic bump-on-a-log characteristic (Grant et al., 2019; Hartmann et al., 2015; Hill et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 3A to C and is consistent with prior studies.

claims.claim: Mural cell coverage of endothelial cells of the capillary bed was incomplete, such that only a few capillary pericytes or thin-stranded capillary processes, if any, were observed in isolated ex vivo preparations.
claims.source: Mural cell coverage of endothelial cells of the capillary bed was incomplete, such that only a few capillary pericytes or thin-stranded capillary processes, if any, were observed in our isolated ex vivo preparations (Grant et al., 2019; Hartmann et al., 2015; Hill et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 3A to C and is consistent with prior studies.

claims.claim: Elastin fibers were observed in the arteriole segment of microvascular preparations, but not in the transitional segment or the capillary region.
claims.source: Elastin fibers were observed in the arteriole segment of our microvascular preparations, but not in the transitional segment or the capillary region (Figure 3D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging data shown in Figure 3D.

claims.claim: The propagation velocity of the vasodilator signal initiated by stimulation of TRPA1 channels in capillaries was significantly slower than that elicited by stimulation of Kir channels.
claims.source: We found that the propagation velocity of signals initiated by stimulation of TRPA1 channels in capillaries was significantly slower than that elicited by stimulation of Kir channels (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by velocity measurements shown in Figure 3E.

claims.claim: TRPA1 channels in brain capillary endothelial cells mediate a signal that dilates upstream arterioles through a mechanism distinct from that initiated by Kir channels.
claims.source: These data imply that TRPA1 channels in brain capillary endothelial cells mediate a signal that dilates upstream arterioles through a mechanism distinct from that initiated by Kir channels.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the different propagation velocities observed.

claims.claim: The propagation velocity of vasodilator signals from the post-arteriole transitional region to the upstream parenchymal arteriole was comparable to that of signals produced by picospritzing capillaries with elevated K+.
claims.source: An analysis of TRPA1-dependent responses in different segments of the cerebral microvasculature showed that the propagation velocity of vasodilator signals from the post-arteriole transitional region (first vascular segment with mural cell coverage) to the upstream parenchymal arteriole was comparable to that of signals produced in this segment by picospritzing capillaries with elevated [K+] (Figure 3F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by velocity measurements shown in Figure 3F.

claims.claim: The signal produced by activation of TRPA1 channels propagates through the capillary network from the site of initiation to the transitional region more slowly than the fast-electrical signal initiated by activation of Kir channels.
claims.source: Consequently, we infer that the signal produced by activation of TRPA1 channels propagates through the capillary network from the site of initiation to the transitional region more slowly than the fast-electrical signal initiated by activation of Kir channels.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the velocity measurements in different vascular segments.

claims.claim: Activation of TRPA1 channels in capillary endothelial cells generates a slowly propagating intercellular signal that is converted to a rapidly conducted electrical signal in vascular segments fully covered by mural cells.
claims.source: We propose a biphasic propagation model of conducted vasodilator signaling in which activation of TRPA1 channels in capillary endothelial cells generates a slowly propagating intercellular signal that is converted to a rapidly conducted electrical signal in vascular segments fully covered by mural cells (Figure 3G).
claims.evidence: This is a model proposed based on the velocity measurements and is illustrated in Figure 3G.

claims.claim: Dilation of upstream parenchymal arterioles following focal application of 4-HNE or AITC to capillary extremities was significantly blunted in ex vivo preparations obtained from Panx1-ecKO mice.
claims.source: We found that dilation of upstream parenchymal arterioles following focal application of 4-HNE or AITC to capillary extremities was significantly blunted in ex vivo preparations obtained from Panx1-ecKO mice compared with those from tamoxifen-injected control mice expressing only Cdh5-Cre as well as vehicle (peanut oil)-injected Panx1-ecKO mice (Figure 4A to C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 4A to C.

claims.claim: Conducted vasodilation initiated by stimulation of Kir channels in brain capillary endothelial cells was not affected by endothelial cell Panx1 knockout.
claims.source: In contrast, conducted vasodilation initiated by stimulation of Kir channels in brain capillary endothelial cells was not affected by endothelial cell Panx1 knockout (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: TRPA1 channels in brain capillary endothelial cells initiate conducted vasodilator responses through an endothelial cell Panx1-dependent mechanism that is independent of the response initiated by Kir channels.
claims.source: These data demonstrate that TRPA1 channels in brain capillary endothelial cells initiate conducted vasodilator responses through an endothelial cell Panx1-dependent mechanism that is independent of the response initiated by Kir channels.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential effects of Panx1 knockout on TRPA1- versus Kir-mediated responses.

claims.claim: Catabolism of extracellular purines with apyrase (1 U/mL) blunted the response to AITC in microvascular preparations from wild-type mice.
claims.source: Pre-incubation of microvascular preparations with apyrase (1 U/mL) to catabolize extracellular purines (Figure 4E) and administration of the pan-P2X inhibitor PPADS (10 µM) blocked the dilation of upstream parenchymal arteriole segments in response to application of AITC to capillaries (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: The pan-P2X inhibitor PPADS (10 µM) blocked the dilation of upstream parenchymal arteriole segments in response to application of AITC to capillaries.
claims.source: Pre-incubation of microvascular preparations with apyrase (1 U/mL) to catabolize extracellular purines (Figure 4E) and administration of the pan-P2X inhibitor PPADS (10 µM) blocked the dilation of upstream parenchymal arteriole segments in response to application of AITC to capillaries (Figure 4F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 4F.

claims.claim: Apyrase and PPADS had no effect on conducted vasodilation initiated by stimulation of brain capillary endothelial cell Kir channels with 10 mM K+.
claims.source: However, apyrase and PPADS had no effect on conducted vasodilation initiated by stimulation of brain capillary endothelial cell Kir channels with 10 mM K+ (Figure 4G and H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 4G and H.

claims.claim: Direct application of ATP onto capillary beds stimulated conducted dilation in preparations from wild-type mice, an effect that was blocked by PPADS.
claims.source: We also found that direct application of ATP onto capillary beds stimulated conducted dilation in preparations from wild-type mice, an effect that was blocked by PPADS (Figure 4I and J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 4I and J.

claims.claim: The velocity of ATP-conducted responses was slower than that of responses initiated by stimulation of Kir channels and was comparable to that of signals produced by stimulation of TRPA1 channels.
claims.source: The velocity of ATP-conducted responses was slower than that of responses initiated by stimulation of Kir channels and was comparable to that of signals produced by stimulation of TRPA1 channels (Figure 4K).
claims.evidence: This is supported by velocity measurements shown in Figure 4K.

claims.claim: Application of ATP onto capillaries did not initiate conducted vasodilation in ex vivo preparations from Panx1-ecKO mice.
claims.source: Consistent with these findings, application of ATP onto capillaries did not initiate conducted vasodilation in ex vivo preparations from Panx1-ecKO mice (Figure 4L).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 4L.

claims.claim: ATP-induced conducted vasodilation persisted in preparations from Trpa1-ecKO mice indicating that TRPA1 is the initiator and that Panx1-P2X signaling is unaffected in these mice.
claims.source: ATP-induced conducted vasodilation persisted in preparations from Trpa1-ecKO mice indicating that TRPA1 is the initiator and that Panx1-P2X signaling is unaffected in these mice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Stimulation of TRPA1 channels on capillary endothelial cells initiates the release of ATP through endothelial cell Panx1 channels.
claims.source: These data support the concept that stimulation of TRPA1 channels on capillary endothelial cells initiates the release of ATP through endothelial cell Panx1 channels.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the pharmacological and genetic experiments.

claims.claim: Released ATP stimulates P2X receptors on adjacent cells to generate a propagating Ca2+ signal.
claims.source: Released ATP, in turn, stimulates P2X receptors on adjacent cells to generate a propagating Ca2+ signal.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the pharmacological experiments and Ca2+ imaging data.

claims.claim: The average capillary endothelial cell length is 28.7 ± 0.6 µm.
claims.source: We found that the average capillary endothelial cell length was 28.7 ± 0.6 µm (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by fluorescence imaging measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A and B.

claims.claim: The length of the capillary segment in ex vivo microvascular preparations is in the range of 100–150 µm.
claims.source: Given that the length of the capillary segment in our ex vivo microvascular preparation is in the range of 100–150 µm (Figure 4—figure supplement 2C)
claims.evidence: This is supported by measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2C.

claims.claim: The signal initiated by TRPA1 channels propagates through 3 to 5 endothelial cells in the capillary network before reaching post-arteriole transitional segments with mural cell coverage.
claims.source: we estimate that the signal initiated by TRPA1 channels propagates through 3 to 5 endothelial cells in the capillary network before reaching post-arteriole transitional segments with mural cell coverage.
claims.evidence: This is an estimate based on the capillary endothelial cell length and the length of the capillary segment.

claims.claim: Focal application of AITC onto the distal extremities of capillaries initiated an increase in intracellular Ca2+ in endothelial cells.
claims.source: Ca2+-imaging studies performed using microvascular preparations obtained from transgenic mice expressing the genetically encoded Ca2+ indicator GCaMP8, exclusively in the endothelium (Cdh5-GCaMP8) (Ohkura et al., 2012) revealed that focal application of AITC onto the distal extremities of capillaries initiated an increase in intracellular [Ca2+] (Video 3).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Video 3 and Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The increase in intracellular Ca2+ triggered by AITC propagates to neighboring regions in the capillary network.
claims.source: Moreover, this increase in intracellular [Ca2+] triggered similar increases in neighboring regions, indicating that the Ca2+ signal propagates through the capillary network (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Figure 5A and Video 3.

claims.claim: AITC-induced Ca2+ signals were abolished by superfusing the preparation with HC-030031.
claims.source: AITC-induced Ca2+ signals were abolished by superfusing the preparation with HC-030031 (Video 4, Figure 5B and C), suggesting that initiation of the signal required the activity of TRPA1 channels.
claims.evidence: This is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Video 4 and Figure 5B and C.

claims.claim: The velocity of vasodilator Ca2+ signals within the capillaries travel at speeds slower than the rapid vasodilator signal traveling through vascular segments covered by mural cells.
claims.source: As expected, the velocity of vasodilator Ca2+ signals within the capillaries travel at speeds slower than the rapid vasodilator signal traveling through vascular segments covered by mural cells (Figure 5D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by velocity measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claims.claim: Focal application of ATP initiated an increase in intracellular Ca2+ that propagates to adjacent cells.
claims.source: Focal application of ATP was also found to initiate an increase in intracellular [Ca2+], that propagates to adjacent cells (Video 5, Figure 5E).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Video 5 and Figure 5E.

claims.claim: PPADS abolished ATP-induced Ca2+ signal, suggesting that initiation and propagation of Ca2+ signals require P2X receptors.
claims.source: PPADS abolished ATP-induced Ca2+ signal, suggesting that initiation and propagation of Ca2+ signals require P2X receptors (Video 6, Figure 5F and G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Video 6 and Figure 5F and G.

claims.claim: The velocity of ATP-induced Ca2+ signals is similar to that produced by activating TRPA1 channels, suggesting a convergent vasodilator signaling pathway.
claims.source: The velocity of ATP-induced Ca2+ signals is similar to that produced by activating TRPA1 channels, suggesting a convergent vasodilator signaling pathway (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by velocity measurements shown in Figure 5H.

claims.claim: ATP-induced Ca2+ signals were abolished in preparations under 0 Ca2+ conditions.
claims.source: We next validated that the vasodilator signal through the capillaries requires influx of extracellular Ca2+ through purinergic P2X receptors by superfusing preparations with aCSF devoid of extracellular Ca2+. We found that ATP-induced Ca2+ signals were abolished in preparations under 0 Ca2+ conditions; however, the response returned once extracellular Ca2+ (2 mM) was reintroduced (Videos 7–9, Figure 5I and J).
claims.evidence: This is supported by Ca2+ imaging data shown in Videos 7–9 and Figure 5I and J.

claims.claim: The propagative Ca2+ signal is dependent on ionotropic purinergic P2X receptor, and not through the release of Ca2+ from intracellular stores downstream of G protein-coupled P2Y receptor activation.
claims.source: This suggests that the propagative Ca2+ signal is dependent on ionotropic purinergic P2X receptor, and not through the release of Ca2+ from intracellular stores downstream of G protein-coupled P2Y receptor activation.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Ca2+ imaging experiments in 0 Ca2+ conditions.

claims.claim: Slow, short-range intercellular Ca2+ signals propagate through capillary endothelial cells via a mechanism that is dependent on ATP release through Panx1 channels and activation of purinergic P2X receptors on adjacent endothelial cells.
claims.source: Taken together, these data support a model in which slow, short-range intercellular Ca2+ signals propagate through capillary endothelial cells via a mechanism that is dependent on ATP release through Panx1 channels and activation of purinergic P2X receptors on adjacent endothelial cells (Figure 5K).
claims.evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data and is illustrated in Figure 5K.

claims.claim: This pathway is necessary for the dilation of upstream arterioles in response to stimulation of TRPA1 channels in capillary endothelial cells.
claims.source: This pathway is necessary for the dilation of upstream arterioles in response to stimulation of TRPA1 channels in capillary endothelial cells.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental data showing the requirement of Panx1 and P2X receptors.

claims.claim: Focal application of elevated K+, 4-HNE, or AITC onto the post-arteriole transitional segment caused dilation of the upstream parenchymal arteriole.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that focal application of elevated [K+], 4-HNE, or AITC onto the post-arteriole transitional segment caused dilation of the upstream parenchymal arteriole (Figure 6B and C), indicating that functional Kir and TRPA1 channels are present in these transitional segments and are capable of producing conducted vasodilator responses when stimulated.
claims.evidence: This is supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claims.claim: Functional Kir and TRPA1 channels are present in post-arteriole transitional segments and are capable of producing conducted vasodilator responses when stimulated.
claims.source: Interestingly, we found that focal application of elevated [K+], 4-HNE, or AITC onto the post-arteriole transitional segment caused dilation of the upstream parenchymal arteriole (Figure 6B and C), indicating that functional Kir and TRPA1 channels are present in these transitional segments and are capable of producing conducted vasodilator responses when stimulated.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the pressure myography data.

claims.claim: The propagation velocities of the conducted vasodilator signals produced by stimulating post-arteriole transitional segment with elevated K+, AITC, or 4-HNE were nearly identical, suggesting a common signal-propagation mechanism.
claims.source: The propagation velocities of the conducted vasodilator signals produced by stimulating post-arteriole transitional segment with elevated [K+], AITC, or 4-HNE were nearly identical, suggesting a common signal-propagation mechanism (Figure 6D).
claims.evidence: This is supported by velocity measurements shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Vasodilator responses to elevated K+ and AITC in the post-arteriole transitional segment were blocked by inhibiting Kir channels with BaCl2.
claims.source: We also found that vasodilator responses to elevated [K+] (Figure 6E) and AITC (Figure 6F) were blocked by inhibiting Kir channels with BaCl2.
claims.evidence: This is supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 6E and F.

claims.claim: Fast electrical communication involving Kir channels is a convergent means of vasodilator signal conduction in vascular segments with mural cell coverage.
claims.source: The rapid signal-propagation velocity and sensitivity to blockade by BaCl2 suggest that fast electrical communication involving Kir channels (Longden et al., 2017) is a convergent means of vasodilator signal conduction in vascular segments with mural cell coverage.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the velocity measurements and pharmacological data.

claims.claim: Superfusing the ex vivo preparation with BaCl2 significantly blunted the response to localized application of AITC onto capillary extremities.
claims.source: We also found that superfusing the ex vivo preparation with BaCl2 significantly blunted the response to localized application of AITC onto capillary extremities (Figure 6G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: Focal application of ATP onto the post-arteriole transitional segment did not evoke dilation of upstream arterioles.
claims.source: Interestingly, focal application of ATP onto the post-arteriole transitional segment did not evoke dilation of upstream arterioles (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B), suggesting that ATP-dependent propagation must be initiated at more distal points in the capillary network.
claims.evidence: This is supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A and B.

claims.claim: Combined inhibition of nitric oxide synthase with L-NAME (100 µM) and cyclooxygenase with indomethacin (10 µM) in microvascular preparations had no effect on arteriole dilation induced by stimulation of capillary extremities with AITC.
claims.source: Combined inhibition of nitric oxide synthase with L-NAME (100 µM) and cyclooxygenase with indomethacin (10 µM) in microvascular preparations had no effect on arteriole dilation induced by stimulation of capillary extremities with AITC (Figure 6H).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 6H.

claims.claim: Inhibition of IK and SK channel activity by superfusing TRAM34 (1 µM) and apamin (300 nM), respectively, significantly blunted upstream dilation in response to focal stimulation of capillary endothelial cell TRPA1 channels.
claims.source: However, inhibition of IK and SK channel activity by superfusing TRAM34 (1 µM) and apamin (300 nM), respectively, significantly blunted upstream dilation in response to focal stimulation of capillary endothelial cell TRPA1 channels (Figure 6I), demonstrating that IK and SK channel activity is necessary for the conducted vasodilator responses initiated by brain capillary endothelial cell TRPA1 channels.
claims.evidence: This is supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 6I.

claims.claim: IK and SK channel activity is necessary for the conducted vasodilator responses initiated by brain capillary endothelial cell TRPA1 channels.
claims.source: However, inhibition of IK and SK channel activity by superfusing TRAM34 (1 µM) and apamin (300 nM), respectively, significantly blunted upstream dilation in response to focal stimulation of capillary endothelial cell TRPA1 channels (Figure 6I), demonstrating that IK and SK channel activity is necessary for the conducted vasodilator responses initiated by brain capillary endothelial cell TRPA1 channels.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the pharmacological data.

claims.claim: IK and SK channels are expressed in post-arteriole transitional segments.
claims.source: Although it has been reported that functional IK and SK channels are not present in capillary endothelial cells (Longden et al., 2017; Figure 1—figure supplement 1), our functional data suggest that IK and SK channels are expressed in post-arteriole transitional segments, where they convert slowly propagating intercellular Ca2+ signals initiated by capillary TRPA1 channels into rapidly propagating electrical signals.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the functional data showing NS309-induced dilation when applied to the transitional segment.

claims.claim: Focal application of NS309 (10 µM) directly onto the post-arteriole transitional segment induced dilation of the upstream parenchymal arteriole.
claims.source: Surprisingly, we found that focal application of NS309 directly onto the post-arteriole transitional segment induced dilation of the upstream parenchymal arteriole, indicating that IK and SK channels are expressed in this region and that their activation results in conducted vasodilation (Figure 6J and K).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 6J and K.

claims.claim: The NS309-induced dilation response in the post-arteriole transitional segment was inhibited by BaCl2.
claims.source: We also found that this response was inhibited by BaCl2 (Figure 6K) and propagated at the same velocity as signals initiated by stimulating the post-arteriole transitional segment with elevated [K+] and TRPA1 agonists (Figure 6L).
claims.evidence: This is supported by pressure myography data shown in Figure 6K.

claims.claim: The NS309-induced response propagated at the same velocity as signals initiated by stimulating the post-arteriole transitional segment with elevated K+ and TRPA1 agonists.
claims.source: We also found that this response was inhibited by BaCl2 (Figure 6K) and propagated at the same velocity as signals initiated by stimulating the post-arteriole transitional segment with elevated [K+] and TRPA1 agonists (Figure 6L).
claims.evidence: This is supported by velocity measurements shown in Figure 6L.

claims.claim: The Ca2+ signals arriving from the capillary network activate IK and SK channels within the post-arteriole transitional segment to initiate a fast-conducting vasodilator response that requires Kir channel activity.
claims.source: These data support the concept that the Ca2+ signals arriving from the capillary network activate IK and SK channels within the post-arteriole transitional segment to initiate a fast-conducting vasodilator response that requires Kir channel activity (Figure 6M).
claims.evidence: This is a model proposed based on the experimental data and is illustrated in Figure 6M.

claims.claim: Local application of AITC (30 µM) onto a capillary produced a significant increase in RBC flux within the stimulated capillary in control Trpa1fl/fl animals.
claims.source: In control Trpa1fl/fl animals, local application of AITC (30 µM) onto a capillary produced a significant increase in RBC flux within the stimulated capillary (Figure 7B and C).
claims.evidence: This is supported by two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 7B and C.

claims.claim: The rate of RBC flux increase following AITC application was 11.6 ± 2.3 RBC/s.
claims.source: The rate of flux increase was 11.6 ± 2.3 RBC/s (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: This is supported by two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: The latency of the RBC flux response to AITC (7.5 ± 1.2 s) was slow compared with the response induced by applying elevated K+ (3.8 ± 0.9 s), as reported by Longden et al., 2017.
claims.source: The latency of this response (7.5 ± 1.2 s, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B) was slow compared with the response induced by applying elevated [K+] (3.8 ± 0.9 s), as reported by Longden et al., 2017.
claims.evidence: This is supported by two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B and comparison to prior published data.

claims.claim: AITC failed to elicit an increase in RBC flux in almost all (6 of 7) Trpa1-ecKO mice tested.
claims.source: In contrast, AITC failed to elicit an increase in RBC flux in almost all (6 of 7) Trpa1-ecKO mice tested (Figure 7D to F).
claims.evidence: This is supported by two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 7D to F.

claims.claim: Local application of AITC onto a capillary significantly increased the cross-sectional area of the upstream arteriole in Trpa1fl/fl animals.
claims.source: We also confirmed vasodilatory responses to capillary stimulation by assessing changes in the cross-sectional area of the feeding arteriole, demonstrating that local application of AITC onto a capillary significantly increased the area of the upstream arteriole in Trpa1fl/fl animals (Figure 7G).
claims.evidence: This is supported by two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 7G.

claims.claim: The increase in cross-sectional area observed in arterioles of Trpa1fl/fl animals was greater than that observed in Trpa1-ecKO mice.
claims.source: Furthermore, the increase in cross-sectional area observed in arterioles of Trpa1fl/fl animals was greater than that observed in Trpa1-ecKO mice (Trpa1fl/fl mice 72.2 ± 10.8 µm2 (n = 11) vs. Trpa1-ecKO mice 8.3 ± 3.9 µm2 (n = 7), p<0.05) (Figure 7H and I).
claims.evidence: This is supported by two-photon imaging data shown in Figure 7H and I.

claims.claim: Activation of endothelial cell TRPA1 channels in the brain dilates upstream arterioles and increases RBC flux in capillaries.
claims.source: These data indicate that activation of endothelial cell TRPA1 channels in the brain dilates upstream arterioles and increases RBC flux in capillaries.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on the two-photon imaging data.

claims.claim: Treatment with HC-030031 (100 mg/kg, i.p. for 30 min) significantly attenuated the increase in cerebral blood flow following whisker stimulation in wild-type mice.
claims.source: To determine if TRPA1 channels are involved in this functional hyperemic response, we treated mice with HC-030031 (100 mg/kg, i.p. for 30 min). HC-030031 treatment significantly attenuated the increase in cerebral blood flow following whisker stimulation (Figure 8A and B).
claims.evidence: This is supported by laser-Doppler flowmetry data shown in Figure 8A and B.

claims.claim: The duration of the hyperemic response was reduced following HC-030031 treatment.
claims.source: Further analysis of the kinetics revealed that the duration of the response was reduced (Figure 8C), and the decay rate was increased (Figure 8D) following HC-030031 treatment, suggesting that TRPA1 channels are needed to sustain the rise in blood flow.

results.result: Native brain capillary endothelial cells express functional TRPA1 channels but not SK/IK channels. Application of 4-HNE (100 nM) elicited dually rectifying currents that were blocked by HC-030031 and absent in Trpa1-ecKO mice, while elevated K+ evoked Kir currents but NS309 had no effect.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C31 provide converging electrophysiological evidence from patch-clamp recordings showing TRPA1 channel function in isolated capillary endothelial cells. The use of pharmacological inhibitors (HC-030031, BaCl2) and genetic knockout controls (Trpa1-ecKO) with appropriate viability checks strengthens the conclusion. The data are internally consistent and use appropriate controls.

results.result: Activation of TRPA1 channels in capillary endothelial cells by 4-HNE or AITC produces conducted vasodilation of upstream arterioles in ex vivo preparations. This response is concentration-dependent (EC50 for 4-HNE: 190 nM; AITC: 6 µM), blocked by HC-030031, requires physical connection between capillaries and arterioles, and is absent in Trpa1-ecKO mice while Kir-mediated responses remain intact.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C45 demonstrate TRPA1-mediated conducted vasodilation through systematic pressure myography experiments with appropriate controls including vehicle (aCSF), physical disconnection, pharmacological inhibition, and genetic knockout. The concentration-response relationships and specificity to TRPA1 (preserved Kir responses in knockout) provide strong evidence. Multiple independent validations support the conclusion.

results.result: Ex vivo microvascular preparations show distinct mural cell morphology across vascular segments: parenchymal arterioles have continuous smooth muscle coverage, post-arteriole transitional segments have ensheathing pericytes with 'bump-on-a-log' morphology, and capillaries have incomplete mural cell coverage. Elastin fibers are present only in arteriole segments.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C49 describe vascular anatomy supported by fluorescence imaging (Figure 3A-D) using established markers (isolectin B4, α-SMA, elastin staining). The findings are consistent with prior literature (Grant et al., 2019; Hartmann et al., 2015; Hill et al., 2015) and provide necessary anatomical context for interpreting functional data.

results.result: TRPA1-initiated vasodilator signals exhibit biphasic propagation: slow propagation through capillaries (~100 µm/s) that is significantly slower than Kir-mediated signals, followed by rapid propagation through post-arteriole transitional segments at velocities comparable to Kir-mediated responses.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C54 present velocity measurements showing distinct propagation speeds in different vascular segments (Figure 3E-F). The biphasic model is supported by quantitative data comparing TRPA1 vs. Kir responses in capillaries versus transitional segments. The inference of signal conversion at the transitional segment is logical given the velocity data, though direct mechanistic proof of the conversion process would strengthen the claim.

results.result: TRPA1-mediated conducted vasodilation requires endothelial Panx1 channels and purinergic P2X receptor signaling. Responses to TRPA1 agonists (but not Kir stimulation) are blocked in Panx1-ecKO mice and by apyrase or PPADS. Direct ATP application mimics TRPA1 responses with similar velocity and is also Panx1-dependent.
results.evaluation: Claims C55-C66 establish the Panx1-P2X signaling pathway through converging genetic (Panx1-ecKO) and pharmacological (apyrase, PPADS) evidence. The specificity is demonstrated by preserved Kir responses and ATP responses in Trpa1-ecKO mice. The similar velocities of TRPA1 and ATP responses support a common pathway. Multiple controls strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: The average capillary endothelial cell length is 28.7 ± 0.6 µm, and capillary segments in ex vivo preparations are 100-150 µm long, suggesting TRPA1-initiated signals propagate through 3-5 endothelial cells before reaching transitional segments.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69 provide morphometric data from fluorescence imaging (Figure 4—figure supplement 2) that allows estimation of cell number in the propagation pathway. The measurements are straightforward and the calculation is reasonable, though the estimate assumes linear propagation and uniform cell spacing.

results.result: TRPA1 activation initiates propagating Ca2+ signals in capillary endothelial cells that are blocked by HC-030031 and travel at slow velocities. ATP application produces similar Ca2+ signals that are blocked by PPADS and abolished in 0 Ca2+ conditions, indicating dependence on P2X receptor-mediated Ca2+ influx rather than intracellular store release.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C80 use Ca2+ imaging in Cdh5-GCaMP8 mice to directly visualize the proposed signaling mechanism. The pharmacological dissection (HC-030031, PPADS) and 0 Ca2+ experiments provide strong mechanistic evidence. The velocity measurements match functional data from pressure myography. The convergence of imaging and functional data strongly supports the Panx1-P2X-Ca2+ signaling model.

results.result: Post-arteriole transitional segments express functional Kir and TRPA1 channels that can initiate conducted vasodilation when directly stimulated. Responses to elevated K+, 4-HNE, or AITC in this segment propagate at similar rapid velocities and are blocked by BaCl2, suggesting convergence onto Kir-mediated electrical signaling. ATP application to transitional segments does not evoke dilation.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C87 demonstrate that transitional segments can both sense stimuli and conduct signals. The similar velocities and BaCl2 sensitivity support electrical propagation as the common mechanism. The lack of ATP response in transitional segments (C87) distinguishes this region from distal capillaries and supports the biphasic model. The data are internally consistent.

results.result: IK and SK channels in post-arteriole transitional segments are necessary for TRPA1-mediated conducted vasodilation. Inhibition with TRAM34 and apamin blocks responses to capillary TRPA1 stimulation, while L-NAME and indomethacin have no effect. Direct NS309 application to transitional segments induces BaCl2-sensitive dilation at velocities matching other stimuli.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C95 identify IK/SK channels as the mechanism converting slow Ca2+ signals to fast electrical signals in transitional segments. The pharmacological evidence (TRAM34, apamin, BaCl2) is clear, and the NS309 experiments directly demonstrate functional IK/SK expression in this segment. This resolves the apparent discrepancy with prior reports of no IK/SK in capillaries (C25, C91). The model in Figure 6M integrates the findings logically.

results.result: In vivo two-photon imaging shows that AITC application to single capillaries increases RBC flux (11.6 ± 2.3 RBC/s) and upstream arteriole cross-sectional area in Trpa1fl/fl mice with a latency of 7.5 ± 1.2 s. These responses are absent in Trpa1-ecKO mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C96-C102 provide critical in vivo validation of the ex vivo findings using two-photon microscopy. The RBC flux and arteriole diameter measurements directly demonstrate functional consequences of TRPA1 activation. The slower latency compared to Kir responses (C98) is consistent with the biphasic propagation model. The genetic control (Trpa1-ecKO) confirms specificity.

results.result: TRPA1 channels contribute to functional hyperemia during prolonged (5 s) but not brief (1-2 s) whisker stimulation in vivo. HC-030031 treatment and Trpa1-ecKO mice show reduced hyperemic response magnitude, duration, and increased decay rate during 5 s stimulation, while rise rate and latency are unaffected. Responses to 1-2 s stimulation are unchanged.
results.evaluation: Claims C103-C112 demonstrate physiological relevance using laser-Doppler flowmetry during sensory stimulation. The kinetic analysis (duration, decay rate vs. rise rate, latency) is appropriate and shows TRPA1 specifically sustains rather than initiates the hyperemic response. The stimulus duration dependence (5 s but not 1-2 s) is consistent with the slow propagation velocity (~7.5 s latency from C98). Both pharmacological and genetic approaches support the conclusion.

results.result: Background claims establishing the physiological context for neurovascular coupling, including the metabolic demands of neurons, constraints on global cerebral blood flow, prior models of NVC (astrocyte-based and Kir-based), and known properties of TRP channels and TRPA1 in cerebral vessels.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C7-C18 provide established background knowledge supported by appropriate citations. These contextual claims are well-documented in the literature and accurately represent current understanding of cerebral hemodynamics and prior NVC models. They appropriately frame the study's rationale.

results.result: Summary claims stating the main findings: TRPA1 channels in capillary endothelial cells initiate retrograde vasodilator signals through biphasic propagation (slow Ca2+-dependent in capillaries via Panx1-P2X, fast electrical in transitional segments via IK/SK/Kir), contributing to functional hyperemia in vivo.
results.evaluation: Claims C2-C6, C19-C23, C118-C121, C155-C158 are high-level summary statements of the study's main findings. These are well-supported by the detailed experimental evidence in other claim groups. The integration of ex vivo mechanistic studies with in vivo functional validation provides strong overall support for the conclusions. The biphasic propagation model is novel and well-substantiated.

results.result: Discussion claims about TRPA1 expression patterns, activation by ROS/4-HNE, and speculation about potential endogenous sources of TRPA1 agonists during NVC (astrocytes, neurons, pericytes, microglia producing ROS).
results.evaluation: Claims C122-C125 cite prior work establishing TRPA1 expression and ROS activation. Claims C126-C129 are speculative hypotheses about endogenous TRPA1 activation during physiological NVC. While the speculation is reasonable given the known biology, no direct evidence is provided that ROS from these sources activates capillary TRPA1 during normal neurovascular coupling. This remains an important open question requiring future investigation.

results.result: Discussion claims about Panx1 channel properties and the proposed mechanism whereby TRPA1-mediated Ca2+ influx triggers ATP release through Panx1, which activates P2X receptors on adjacent cells to propagate Ca2+ signals, similar to mechanisms in other cell types.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C134 cite established knowledge about Panx1-P2X signaling in other systems and propose a similar mechanism operates in brain capillaries, which is supported by the experimental data (claims C55-C80). Claim C135 is supported by the data. Claim C136 is reasonable speculation about other potential Ca2+ sources but lacks direct evidence.

results.result: Discussion claims about purinergic signaling in vascular control, including ATP release from nerves and endothelium, and speculation that ATP from astrocytes/neurons could activate capillary endothelial P2X receptors to initiate Panx1-dependent vasodilation.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C143 cite established knowledge about purinergic signaling. Claim C141 is supported by the experimental data. Claim C144 is a speculative model proposing that neuronal/astrocytic ATP could directly activate the capillary endothelial Panx1-P2X pathway. While the data show exogenous ATP can activate this pathway (C61, C74), there is no direct evidence that endogenous ATP from neurons/astrocytes does so during physiological NVC. This hypothesis requires testing.

results.result: Discussion claims about the importance of post-arteriole transitional segments for NVC, their composition (ensheathing pericytes), their dual role as sensors and signal converters, and speculation that transitional segment endothelial cells are phenotypically distinct from capillary endothelial cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C145-C151 are supported by the functional data showing transitional segments can sense stimuli (C81-C82) and convert slow Ca2+ signals to fast electrical signals (C95, C151). Claims C146-C148 cite established anatomy. Claim C152 is reasonable speculation based on functional differences (IK/SK expression) but acknowledges that molecular verification is needed. The conclusions about transitional segment function are well-supported.

results.result: Discussion claims about the clinical relevance of understanding NVC mechanisms for neurological disorders and how the capillary-centric view has changed understanding of functional hyperemia.
results.evaluation: Claims C153-C154 provide appropriate context about the broader significance of NVC research. C153 is established knowledge about cerebrovascular dysfunction in disease. C154 accurately references the paradigm shift introduced by Longden et al., 2017. These contextual claims are well-supported.

results.result: Discussion claims about brain capillary density, neuronal proximity to capillaries, the capillary network as a sensory web for K+, and the inference that multiple complementary sensors must exist in capillary endothelial cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C115 cite established anatomical knowledge (Tsai and Kleinfeld, 2009; Longden et al., 2017). Claim C116 is established knowledge. Claim C117 is a logical inference from the essential nature of NVC and the complexity of brain signaling, which is supported by the demonstration of TRPA1 as an additional sensor beyond Kir channels.
